prompt: While modeling shopping mall operations, a team is documenting this statement: "When a customer submits a return, the stock quantity of the product increases and the payment amount is refunded." Which modeling perspective does this description mainly correspond to?
explanation: Looking at how data (stock quantity, payment amount) is affected by business processing (accepting a return) is the interaction perspective between data and process. The data perspective in A looks at which data the business is related to (what is stored for customers, products, and orders). The process perspective in C looks at what the business actually does (accepting the return itself) and does not examine its effect on the data. Conceptual modeling in D is the name of a modeling stage (conceptual, logical, physical), not one of the three perspectives.

prompt: Four entity candidates were identified in a shopping mall business analysis. Considering the characteristics of an entity, which one is the LEAST likely to be an entity?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: A set whose discount rates by membership grade are defined in advance and referenced every time an order is placed

choices.label: C
choices.text: A set that manages product inquiries left by customers, distinguished by inquiry number

choices.label: D
choices.text: A set that records each product receipt, assigned a receipt number every time a product is received

explanation: An entity must have two or more instances. The operating company information is only a single record, so it does not meet the conditions of an entity. B has multiple grades as instances and is referenced by order processing, so it can be a concept entity. C distinguishes multiple inquiries by an identifier called the inquiry number and has relationships with products and customers. D also has multiple receipt records identified by receipt numbers, which are created by the business process.

prompt: Among the attributes of the shopping mall Order entity, which one is a designed attribute in the classification by characteristics?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cumulative purchase amount (the sum of payments made so far)

choices.label: D

explanation: A designed attribute is one that does not originally exist in the business but is newly created during design. The order status code, which defines "received, shipping, delivered" as the codes `10`, `20`, `30`, falls into this category. A and D are basic attributes taken directly from business analysis. B is a value obtained by summing another attribute (payment amount), so it is a derived attribute.

prompt: In a relationship line drawn in Barker notation between Product Category and Product, the half on the Product Category side is a dashed line, the half on the Product side is a solid line, and there is a crow's foot at the Product end. Which is the correct interpretation of this relationship?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One product belongs to multiple categories, and there may be products without a category

choices.label: B
choices.text: One category has multiple products, and there may be products without a category

choices.label: C
choices.text: One product has multiple categories, and there cannot be a category without products

choices.label: D
choices.text: One category has multiple products, and there may be categories without products

explanation: In Barker notation, optionality is expressed by the line style of each entity's own half. The category half is dashed, so category participation is optional (a category without products is possible); the product half is solid, so product participation is mandatory (every product belongs to a category). The crow's foot is on the product side, so one category has multiple products. A and C read the direction of the crow's foot in reverse. B gets the cardinality right but misreads the solid line on the product side (mandatory) as optional.

prompt: The Employee entity has employee number (primary identifier), national ID number, and department number (received through a relationship from the Department entity). Other entities use only the employee number when referencing an employee. Which statement about the identifiers of this entity is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national ID number distinguishes employees but is not used for references, so it is an alternate identifier

choices.label: B
choices.text: The department number is a value created within the Employee entity itself, so it is an internal identifier

choices.label: C
choices.text: The employee number consists of a single attribute, so it fails the minimality of a primary identifier

choices.label: D
choices.text: The national ID number also distinguishes employees, so other entities must receive it as a FK

explanation: An identifier that can distinguish instances but lacks representativeness and is not used to connect referencing relationships is an alternate identifier. B is wrong. The department number is a foreign identifier received through the relationship with Department. C misunderstands minimality. Minimality means using only as many attributes as needed for uniqueness, and a single attribute naturally satisfies it. D is the opposite of the nature of an alternate identifier. An alternate identifier is used as a search condition or a UNIQUE constraint and is not received as a FK by other entities.

prompt:
The primary identifier of the Order entity is order number, and its attributes are order date, customer number, and customer grade. All attributes are atomic values. Part of the data is as follows.
(Order number 5001, Order date 2026-11-01, Customer number C01, Customer grade GOLD)
(Order number 5002, Order date 2026-11-02, Customer number C01, Customer grade GOLD)
(Order number 5003, Order date 2026-11-02, Customer number C02, Customer grade SILVER)
The functional dependencies are `order number -> order date, customer number` and `customer number -> customer grade`. What is the lowest normal form that this entity does NOT satisfy?
explanation: Since order number -> customer number and customer number -> customer grade, order number -> customer grade is a transitive functional dependency. A regular attribute (customer grade) depends on another regular attribute (customer number), so 3NF is not satisfied, and customer number and customer grade must be separated into a Customer entity. That is why GOLD for C01 is repeated as many times as there are orders. D is wrong. All attributes are atomic values, so 1NF is satisfied. A is also wrong. The primary identifier is a single attribute, so a partial functional dependency cannot occur and 2NF is satisfied. BCNF in C is not satisfied either, but 3NF is violated first, so it is not the lowest normal form.

prompt: In a performance reservation model, Reservation and Reserved Seat have a mandatory relationship on both sides. choices.label: A
choices.text: COMMIT the reservation first, and save the seats in a separate transaction on the next screen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Group the reservation INSERT and the reserved seat INSERT into one transaction and COMMIT them together

choices.label: C
choices.text: Save and COMMIT the reserved seats first, and save the reservation information separately after payment is fully completed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the two entities have a mandatory relationship, the DBMS automatically merges the two rows into one table

choices.label: B
choices.text: Define a separate UNIQUE constraint on (student ID, course number, semester)

choices.label: C
choices.text: Define the Enrollment ID column as NOT NULL to prevent empty values

choices.label: D
choices.text: Create one more regular index on the Enrollment ID column in addition to the PK index

explanation: A surrogate identifier gets a new value for every row, so even for the same (student ID, course number, semester) combination the PK differs and the DBMS does not block it. To prevent duplicates, a separate UNIQUE constraint (index) must be placed on the essential columns, at the cost of having two indexes. A overlooks exactly this point. C is wrong because a PK is already NOT NULL, and preventing empty Enrollment ID values does not prevent duplicates in the essential columns. D only adds an index on Enrollment ID and has nothing to do with duplicates of the essential column combination.

explanation: MINUS removes from the upper result the values that are in the lower result. Removing CLERK and MANAGER, which are also in department 10, from the department 30 jobs leaves only SALESMAN. PRESIDENT in B is the result of the swapped `department 10 MINUS department 30`. C is the result of the INTERSECT set operator. D: There is a job only in department 30, so it is not 0 rows.

prompt: Which of the following SQL statements runs in Oracle without error?

choices.label: A
choices.text: SELECT EMPNO FROM EMP UNION SELECT ENAME FROM EMP;

choices.label: B
choices.text: SELECT EMPNO, ENAME FROM EMP UNION SELECT DEPTNO FROM DEPT;

choices.label: C
choices.text: SELECT DEPTNO FROM DEPT ORDER BY DEPTNO UNION ALL SELECT DEPTNO FROM EMP;

choices.label: D
choices.text: SELECT DEPTNO, NULL FROM DEPT UNION SELECT DEPTNO, ENAME FROM EMP;

explanation: D has 2 columns on both the upper and lower sides, and NULL matches any data type, so it can correspond to ENAME. Running it returns 18 rows. A fails with ORA-01790 because the numeric EMPNO and the character ENAME are of different data type families. B has 2 columns above and 1 column below, so the column counts differ, giving ORA-01789. C places ORDER BY after the first SELECT. In a set operation, ORDER BY can be written only once, at the very end.

prompt:
The jobs in department 10 are CLERK, MANAGER, and PRESIDENT, and the jobs in department 20 are ANALYST, CLERK, and MANAGER. What is the number of result rows of the following SQL?
SELECT DEPTNO, JOB, COUNT(*)
FROM EMP
WHERE DEPTNO IN (10, 20)
GROUP BY CUBE(DEPTNO, JOB);
explanation: CUBE creates every possible grouping. (department, job) 6 rows + by department 2 rows + by job 4 rows (ANALYST, CLERK, MANAGER, PRESIDENT) + grand total 1 row = 13 rows. The 9 in B is the result of ROLLUP, which has no per-job subtotals. The 12 in C omits the grand total. The 16 in D counts the per-job subtotals again for each department; CUBE does not create the same grouping twice.

prompt:
The CLERK salaries are SMITH 800, ADAMS 1100 (both in department 20), JAMES 950 (department 30), and MILLER 1300 (department 10). In the result of the following SQL, what are the SUM(SAL), G1, and G2 values of the row where DEPTNO is NULL and JOB is CLERK?
SELECT DEPTNO, JOB, SUM(SAL),
       GROUPING(DEPTNO) AS G1, GROUPING(JOB) AS G2
FROM EMP
GROUP BY CUBE(DEPTNO, JOB);
explanation: The row where DEPTNO is NULL and JOB is CLERK is the per-job subtotal, with department collapsed and grouped by job only. The sum of the salaries of the 4 CLERKs is 4150, the collapsed DEPTNO has GROUPING 1, and JOB, which is grouped by its actual value, has 0. A is the value of the grand total row, where both columns are collapsed. B reads the 1 and 0 of GROUPING backwards. GROUPING is 1 for a column collapsed by aggregation. The 1900 in C is the sum for department 20 CLERKs only.

prompt:
The hire dates in department 10 are CLARK 1981-06-09, KING 1981-11-17, and MILLER 1982-01-23, the first hire in department 20 is SMITH (1980-12-17), and the first hire in department 30 is ALLEN (1981-02-20). What is the result of the following SQL?
SELECT ENAME
FROM (SELECT ENAME,
             ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY DEPTNO ORDER BY HIREDATE) AS RN
      FROM EMP)
WHERE RN = 1
ORDER BY ENAME;
explanation: PARTITION BY DEPTNO restarts the numbering from 1 in hire date order for each department, and outside the inline view only number 1 is kept. These are CLARK in department 10, SMITH in department 20, and ALLEN in department 30, sorted by name. A picks KING, the highest-ranking employee in department 10. B is the result if numbered in descending hire date order. D is the employee who is number 1 overall when there is no PARTITION BY.

prompt:
The SALESMAN salaries are ALLEN 1600, TURNER 1500, MARTIN 1250, and WARD 1250. What is the S value in the result of the following SQL?
SELECT ENAME, SUM(SAL) OVER (PARTITION BY JOB) AS S
FROM EMP
WHERE ENAME = 'ALLEN';
explanation: A window function is computed in the SELECT stage on the rows left after WHERE. WHERE leaves only the one row for ALLEN, so the SALESMAN partition also has just one row, ALLEN, and the sum is 1600. The 5600 in B assumes all 4 SALESMAN were added before WHERE. The 29025 in C is the sum of all salaries in EMP. D: ORA-30483 occurs when a window function is used in the WHERE clause, but here it is used in the SELECT clause.

prompt:
Viewing department 20 in hire date order gives SMITH (800), JONES (2975), FORD (3000), SCOTT (3000), and ADAMS (1100). In the result of the following SQL, what is the L value in the SCOTT row?
SELECT ENAME, LEAD(SAL, 2, 0) OVER (ORDER BY HIREDATE) AS L
FROM EMP
WHERE DEPTNO = 20
ORDER BY HIREDATE;
explanation: `LEAD(SAL, 2, 0)` fetches the salary two rows later, and uses the default value 0 if there is no such row. After SCOTT there is only one row, ADAMS, so the value is 0. The 1100 in A is the value one row later (ADAMS), which is also the L value in the FORD row. B: The result would be NULL if the default were omitted, but here 0 was given. The 3000 in D is the value of the immediately preceding row (FORD), as if looking backward like `LAG(SAL, 1)`.

prompt:
The most recently hired employee is ADAMS (1987-05-23), the next is SCOTT (1987-04-19), and the earliest hired employee is SMITH (1980-12-17). What is the result of the following SQL?
SELECT ENAME
FROM (SELECT ENAME FROM EMP ORDER BY HIREDATE DESC)
WHERE ROWNUM <= 2;
explanation: The inline view first sorts by hire date in descending order, and the outer ROWNUM assigns 1 and 2 in that order, leaving two rows. The order is ADAMS, SCOTT. B is the first two employees when sorted in ascending order. C assumes the order is reversed outside, but the order of the inline view carries through. D: `ROWNUM <= 2` stops at exactly 2 rows.

prompt:
Viewing EMP in ascending salary order gives SMITH 800, JAMES 950, ADAMS 1100, MARTIN 1250, WARD 1250, MILLER 1300, and so on. What is the number of result rows of the following SQL?
SELECT ENAME, SAL
FROM EMP
ORDER BY SAL
FETCH FIRST 4 ROWS WITH TIES;
explanation: `WITH TIES` also returns the rows whose ORDER BY value is the same as that of the nth row. The employees with the same salary as the 4th row, 1250, are MARTIN and WARD, so there are 5 rows. The 4 in A is the result of `ROWS ONLY`. C includes MILLER, who has the next salary of 1300. D: FETCH FIRST is applied normally after ORDER BY, so not all 14 rows are returned.

prompt:
BLAKE has 5 subordinates, ALLEN, WARD, MARTIN, TURNER, and JAMES, and they have no subordinates. What is the result of the following SQL?
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM EMP
START WITH ENAME = 'BLAKE'
CONNECT BY PRIOR EMPNO = MGR;
explanation: START WITH sets BLAKE as the root, and `PRIOR EMPNO = MGR` traverses downward from parent to child. The root BLAKE 1 row + 5 subordinate rows = 6 rows. B misses that the root row is included in the result. The 1 in C counts only the root BLAKE, missing that the child rows are attached. D is the number of rows when expanding with KING as the root.

prompt:
Under KING are JONES, BLAKE, and CLARK; under JONES are SCOTT and FORD; under SCOTT is ADAMS; and under FORD is SMITH. Under BLAKE are 5 employees, and under CLARK is MILLER. What is the result of the following SQL?
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM EMP
WHERE LEVEL = 3
START WITH MGR IS NULL
CONNECT BY PRIOR EMPNO = MGR;
explanation: For LEVEL, the root KING is 1, and JONES, BLAKE, and CLARK are 2. LEVEL 3 consists of SCOTT and FORD, BLAKE's 5 subordinates, and MILLER, for 8 employees. The 2 in A is the number of LEVEL 4 employees, ADAMS and SMITH. The 3 in C is the number at LEVEL 2. The 10 in D counts everything at LEVEL 3 and above.

prompt:
The salaries by job are: department 10 CLERK 1300 and MANAGER 2450; department 20 CLERK 800 and 1100 and MANAGER 2975; department 30 CLERK 950 and MANAGER 2850. In the result of the following SQL, what are the C and M values of the row where DEPTNO is 20?
SELECT *
FROM (SELECT DEPTNO, JOB, SAL FROM EMP)
PIVOT (MAX(SAL) FOR JOB IN ('CLERK' AS C, 'MANAGER' AS M))
ORDER BY DEPTNO;
explanation: PIVOT creates one column for each JOB value in FOR and computes MAX(SAL) grouped by the remaining column, DEPTNO. The maximum for department 20 CLERK is 1100 and for MANAGER is 2975. The 1900 in B is the value when aggregated with SUM. The 800 in C is the MIN value. D reads the IN list order and column order backwards. The columns appear in the order written in the IN list (C, M).

prompt:
The JOBs in EMP are 4 CLERK, 4 SALESMAN, 3 MANAGER, 2 ANALYST, and 1 PRESIDENT. What is the result of the following SQL?
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM EMP
WHERE REGEXP_LIKE(JOB, 'MAN$');
explanation: `$` means the end of the string, so 'MAN$' finds values ending in MAN. Only the 4 SALESMAN match. The 7 in A counts every MANAGER and SALESMAN, which contain MAN somewhere, as if there were no `$`. The 3 in B is the result of `'^MAN'`, which matches values starting with MAN. The 0 in C assumes the whole string must be equal, as in `LIKE 'MAN'`, but REGEXP_LIKE is true if the pattern appears anywhere.

prompt:
In TEX4_EMP, a copy of EMP, KING's SAL is 5000 and COMM is NULL. After running the following statement, what are KING's SAL and COMM?
UPDATE TEX4_EMP SET SAL = SAL + 100, COMM = SAL WHERE ENAME = 'KING';

choices.label: C
choices.text: An error occurs because the same column is referenced twice in SET

explanation: Columns on the right side of SET in an UPDATE use their values before the change. SAL becomes 5000 + 100 = 5100, and COMM receives 5000, the SAL before the change. A is the answer that assumes SET is applied from the left in sequence and reads the changed SAL. B is the answer that assumes the SAL change was not applied. Changing a column once on the left side of SET and reading it on the right side is allowed, so C is also wrong.

prompt:
TEX4_BONUS contains 3 employees of department 10 (CLARK SAL 2450, KING 5000, MILLER 1300) with BONUS = SAL. Department 20 has 5 employees. After running the following MERGE, what is the number of rows in TEX4_BONUS?
MERGE INTO TEX4_BONUS B
USING (SELECT EMPNO, ENAME, SAL FROM EMP WHERE DEPTNO IN (10, 20)) E
ON (B.EMPNO = E.EMPNO)
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET B.BONUS = E.SAL * 0.1 DELETE WHERE (B.BONUS > 400)
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT (EMPNO, ENAME, BONUS) VALUES (E.EMPNO, E.ENAME, 0);

choices.label: D
choices.text: An error occurs because DELETE cannot be used inside MERGE

explanation: The 3 employees of department 10 are MATCHED, so BONUS is changed to 10% of SAL (245, 500, 130). Then DELETE WHERE deletes KING, whose changed BONUS is > 400. The 5 employees of department 20 are NOT MATCHED, so they are INSERTed. 3 - 1 + 5 = 7. A is the answer that ignores DELETE WHERE. B is the answer that assumes only the UPDATE happened without the INSERT. Since Oracle 10g, DELETE WHERE can be appended to the MATCHED clause, so D is also wrong.

prompt: Which statement about Oracle's MERGE statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rows that are not in the source but only in the target are deleted by MERGE

choices.label: B
choices.text: It runs even with only a WHEN NOT MATCHED clause

choices.label: C
choices.text: A target column used in the ON clause can also be changed with UPDATE SET

choices.label: D
choices.text: The target table name must be written again inside the UPDATE and INSERT clauses

explanation: Since Oracle 10g, you may write just one of WHEN MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED (in 9i both were required). MERGE runs based on the source and neither deletes nor changes rows that exist only in the target, so A is wrong. Changing a column used in the ON clause with UPDATE SET raises ORA-38104, so C is wrong. Inside MERGE you write `UPDATE SET …` and `INSERT (…) VALUES (…)` directly without repeating the table name, so D is also wrong.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ROLLBACK after TRUNCATE raises an error and TEX4_A has 4 rows

explanation: TRUNCATE is DDL, so it implicitly COMMITs the transaction that was open before it ran. This is true even for DDL on a different table, so the DELETE on TEX4_A (2 rows) is also committed. The ROLLBACK afterward has nothing to undo, so TEX4_A has 2 rows. A is the answer that does not take the automatic commit of DDL into account. B is the answer that assumes TRUNCATE was applied to TEX4_A as well. ROLLBACK completes without error even if there are no changes to undo, so D is also wrong.

prompt: Session 1 UPDATEs a row and has not yet COMMITted. If session 2 then SELECTs the same row, it sees the value before the change. Which transaction property is most closely related to this behavior?
explanation: Isolation is what prevents other transactions from seeing the intermediate results of a running transaction. Session 2 cannot see the change before COMMIT and sees the value before the change. Atomicity is the property that all operations of a transaction are applied or none are. Durability is the property that committed results remain after a failure. Consistency is the property that data obeys rules such as constraints before and after execution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All constraints are copied, so the four INSERTs fail and the result is 1, 1

explanation: When copying with CTAS, only the NOT NULL constraint carries over, and PRIMARY KEY, CHECK, and DEFAULT are dropped. The duplicate ID 1 goes in because there is no PK, and QTY -1 also goes in because there is no CHECK. Only the row that puts NULL in NM fails with ORA-01400 because of NOT NULL. The last row has no DEFAULT, so QTY is NULL. So COUNT(*) is 4 and COUNT(QTY) is 3. A assumes NOT NULL is dropped too and DEFAULT 0 remains. B assumes PK, CHECK, and DEFAULT are all copied (the duplicate ID 1, NULL, and -1 rows fail, and the ID 4 row goes in with QTY 0, giving 2 rows). D assumes all constraints are copied, but even so the ID 4 row would go in, so it does not hold.

prompt: There is TEX4_EMP, a CTAS copy of the EMPNO, ENAME, and SAL of department 10 (CLARK, KING, MILLER) in EMP. ENAME is VARCHAR2(10). Which of the following statements causes an error?

choices.label: B
choices.text: ALTER TABLE TEX4_EMP ADD (GRADE NUMBER DEFAULT 1 NOT NULL);

choices.label: C
choices.text: ALTER TABLE TEX4_EMP RENAME COLUMN SAL TO SALARY;

explanation: CLARK (5 characters) and MILLER (6 characters) are longer than 4 bytes, so the MODIFY that shortens the length fails with ORA-01441. In B, DEFAULT is given as well, so the existing 3 rows are filled with 1, and a NOT NULL column can be added even when rows exist. C is valid syntax for renaming a column. A MODIFY that increases the length, as in D, always works.

choices.label: D
choices.text: NULL cannot be inserted into UNIQUE and CHECK columns, so 1

explanation: UNIQUE does not treat NULLs as equal to each other, so column A can accept multiple rows with NULL. CHECK blocks only when the condition is FALSE and lets through the UNKNOWN produced by a NULL comparison. So the first three rows go in. (1, 3) fails with ORA-00001 because A=1 already exists, and (2, 0) fails with ORA-02290 because B > 0 is false. A and D are answers that treat NULL as a UNIQUE or CHECK violation. B misses either the UNIQUE violation or the CHECK violation.

prompt: User A gave B a privilege with `GRANT CREATE TABLE TO B WITH ADMIN OPTION;`, and B gave C the CREATE TABLE privilege. Then A ran `REVOKE CREATE TABLE FROM B;`. What is the result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The privileges of both B and C are revoked together

choices.label: B
choices.text: The REVOKE fails because C still holds the privilege

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only B's privilege is revoked, and C keeps theirs

choices.label: D
choices.text: B's privilege remains and only C's privilege is revoked

explanation: CREATE TABLE is a system privilege, and revoking a system privilege received with WITH ADMIN OPTION does not cascade. Only B's privilege disappears, and the privilege B gave to C remains. A, in which both are revoked together, is the behavior when an object privilege was granted with WITH GRANT OPTION. REVOKE does not fail even if privileges were given to other users, so B is also wrong. The target of REVOKE is B, so D is also wrong.

prompt: SCOTT wants to give KIM the SELECT and UPDATE privileges on his own EMP table, while allowing KIM to grant these privileges to other users again. Which statement is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: GRANT SELECT, UPDATE ON EMP TO KIM WITH ADMIN OPTION;

choices.label: B
choices.text: GRANT SELECT, UPDATE TO KIM ON EMP WITH GRANT OPTION;

choices.label: C
choices.text: GRANT SELECT, UPDATE ON EMP FROM KIM WITH GRANT OPTION;

choices.label: D
choices.text: GRANT SELECT, UPDATE ON EMP TO KIM WITH GRANT OPTION;

explanation: Object privileges are granted in the order `GRANT privilege ON object TO user`, and to allow re-granting you attach WITH GRANT OPTION. WITH ADMIN OPTION is an option attached to system privileges, so A is wrong. In B, ON object comes after TO, so the syntax order is wrong. FROM is the keyword used in REVOKE, while GRANT uses TO, so C is also wrong.
